composition: Nominal composition of S1 (wt.%, balance Fe): C 0.98, Al 6.00, Mn 0.99, Si 0.33, Mo 0.49, B 0.0036; Ni and Ti were not deliberately added. Design intent: Al at ~6 wt.% is the primary low-density element (≈1.3 % density reduction per wt.% Al) and simultaneously stabilizes ferrite, accelerates the bainitic transformation and refines bainitic lamellae during low-temperature austempering; Mn is limited to ≈1 wt.% and Si kept low at 0.33 wt.% because Al already suppresses carbide precipitation. The high C content (~1 wt.%) is required to achieve full austenitization without polygonal ferrite (αp) and to hold the martensite-start temperature near 300 °C; Mo is added for hardenability and B microalloying further raises hardenability without harming the bainitic transformation. S1 belongs to the Al ≥ 6 wt.% group (S1–S3) of the study.
conclusions: Within the study's comparison of five low-density Al–C nano-bainitic steels, S1 austempered at 300 °C represents the strongest condition: it gives the highest Rp0.2 (1225 MPa) of the whole set together with UTS ≈1600 MPa at 6.8 % elongation (PSE 10,880 MPa·%). The Al ≥ 6 wt.% alloys S1 and S2 transform at an intermediate-fast rate (Bt 1600–4000 s), much faster than the 8.08 wt.% Al steel S3 (Bt 14,000–43,000 s) but slower than the low-C, moderate-Al S5 (700–1000 s), while Ti-microalloyed S4 shows rapid initial nucleation later slowed by bainitic sheaf impingement (Bt 3000–3500 s). Carbide analysis confirms that (Fe,M)xCy and TiMoC form mainly above the austempering temperature and that in S1–S3 the (Fe,M)xCy particles produce no micro-voids and have negligible direct influence on tensile properties. Overall the work shows that TB primarily tunes the strength–ductility trade-off through plate thickness and retained-austenite stability, that C variations near 1 wt.% are secondary to the Al level in setting that balance, and that alloy composition and microstructural features (as supported by MatCalc TTP modelling) govern the bainitic transformation and the resulting strength–ductility response of low-density, high-strength steels.
mechanisms: Al alloying suppresses carbide precipitation (lowering C activity and diffusivity in austenite), stabilizes ferrite and refines bainitic lamellae at low austempering temperature, which together enable the nano-scale bainitic microstructure (Lt(t) = 35 nm) at 300 °C.

Austempering just above Ms (TB = 300 °C vs Ms = 277 °C) suppresses the intermediate/martensitic transformations, so the austenite decomposes isothermally to nano-bainitic ferrite with the transformation completing after about 4000 s (incubation 80 s).

Lowering TB from 350 °C to 300 °C reduces the bainitic lamellar thickness from 55 nm (SD 23) to 35 nm (SD 11); the finer plates and the associated denser defect/interface population raise UTS and Rp0.2 but reduce elongation.

Higher TB raises the retained-austenite fraction (34 % at 350 °C vs 27 % at 300 °C in S1) because more C partitions into the untransformed austenite and chemically stabilizes it, promoting an incomplete-reaction character; the reduced Vγ at 300 °C limits TRIP-assisted strain hardening and thus lowers elongation.

The rounded (Fe,M)xCy (M = Si, Mo) carbides nucleate rapidly and spherically at the γr–bainitic ferrite boundaries; their accelerated nucleation and non-brittle, void-free interfaces give them a negligible effect on the tensile properties, unlike the embrittling behaviour usually expected from Fe₃C.

Si trapped inside the carbide lattice by rapid cooling (under equilibrium Si does not dissolve in Fe₃C) and Mo incorporated into the particles enhance their stability, which further inhibits micro-void formation at the precipitates.

TTP simulations place (Fe,M)xCy precipitation between roughly 700 °C and 1150 °C during cooling of S1 with extremely fast nucleation kinetics, so their formation is unavoidable and occurs primarily during prior processing/cooling rather than during the austempering hold (secondary precipitation requires impractically long times at TB due to limited diffusivity).

The high-C–Al alloying design raises Ms and narrows the austenite single-phase field, which is why a high C level (~1 wt.%) and an austenitizing temperature of 1150 °C (above the 991 °C simulated and 1062 °C measured ferrite-free TA) are needed to eliminate polygonal ferrite and dissolve carbides before the bainitic hold.
microstructure: After austenitizing at 1150 °C and austempering at 300 °C, S1 exhibits an αp-free nano-bainitic (nB) microstructure (LOM at 1150 °C labelled "αp-free"; αp recorded as "–" in Table 3) composed of three phases: nano-bainitic ferrite (fine parallel needle/lath bainite forming type 1 and type 2 nB sheaves), fcc retained austenite (γr, 27 vol.%) present largely as blocky regions between bainite sheaves (contrast with the higher 34 vol.% at TB = 350 °C), and cementite-like (Fe,M)xCy carbides with M = Si, Mo. True bainitic lamellar thickness Lt(t) is 35 nm with a standard deviation of 11 nm (vs 55 nm/SD 23 at 350 °C), i.e. the lower austempering temperature refines the plates and narrows their thickness spread. Rietveld micro-strains are εγ = 0.50 % and εα = 0.45 %. The rounded (Fe,M)xCy particles sit near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries and are only detectable through localized brightness in SEM; they form with accelerated nucleation and a spherical morphology, leaving no micro-voids at the particle interfaces. No κ-carbide plates were observed (attributed to the limited ~1 wt.% Mn), so any κ-carbide is presumed to persist only as nanoscale, non-stoichiometric L1₂-type structures in the matrix. The γr–bainitic ferrite interface is the main phase boundary of this state.
processing: Processing lineage (process_id proc_ta1150-tb300): (1) vacuum arc furnace casting of steel blocks; (2) homogenization at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to even out composition and microstructure; (3) step-by-step hot rolling reducing thickness to ~11 mm, followed by slow cooling in the oven; (4) water-jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, Washington, USA) to precise geometries and cylindrical specimens of ø5×10 mm³ to minimize thermal distortion; (5)–(8) heat treatment in a DIL 805A dilatometer following the Fig. 1(a) cycle: heating at 10 K s⁻¹ to 1150 °C, isothermal austenitization for 15 min, continuous cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ (fast enough to suppress intermediate transformations and ensure fine bainitic transformation) to the austempering temperature TB = 300 °C, isothermal bainitic hold of 4000 s (the near-full transformation duration Bt for this condition, with an incubation time of 80 s), then final cooling. The austenitizing temperature of 1150 °C was fixed for S1, S2, S4 and S5 and selected above both the MatCalc ferrite-free TA (991 °C) and the dilatometrically measured TA (1062 °C) so that the microstructure is αp-free and carbides are dissolved; TB = 300 °C was chosen just above the measured Ms of 277 °C to promote bainite and suppress martensite.
properties: Mechanical response (all specimens heat-treated in the DIL 805A dilatometer and tested on a Zwick/Roell universal machine with a 250 kN load cell using ASTM E8 sub-size round specimens, 12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length): yield strength Rp0.2 = 1225 MPa (the maximum among all investigated conditions), ultimate tensile strength ≈1600 MPa, total elongation 6.8 %, giving a product of strength and elongation (PSE) of 10,880 MPa·%; hardness 497 HV30. Transformational characteristics from dilatometry: Ms = 277 °C, incubation time 80 s, near-full bainitic transformation time Bt = 4000 s at 300 °C. Comparison with the same alloy at TB = 350 °C shows that lowering TB to 300 °C increases strength (UTS ≈1600 vs ≈1380 MPa) and hardness while reducing elongation (6.8 % vs 8.7 %) and PSE (~10,880 vs ~12,000 MPa·%). Characterization techniques applied to this sample: light optical microscopy (LOM, 6 % Nital etching), SEM, EDX, EBSD, XRD (Malvern Panalytical Empyrean, Cu Kα, 40 kV/40 mA; Rietveld refinement of Vγ and micro-strain per ASTM E975-13), MatCalc equilibrium and precipitation-kinetics (TTP) simulations, dilatometry (DIL 805A), tensile testing (ASTM E8) and HV30 hardness.
summary: S1 (alloy_s1) is a high-carbon, high-aluminium low-density steel (Fe–0.98C–6.00Al–0.99Mn–0.33Si–0.49Mo–0.0036B, wt.%) that was vacuum-arc cast, homogenized, hot rolled and then austenitized at 1150 °C for 15 min and austempered at 300 °C for 4000 s in a dilatometer to obtain an αp-free nano-bainitic (nB) microstructure. The core research question is how C–Al alloying and austempering temperature govern bainitic transformation kinetics, the resulting nano-bainitic/retained-austenite microstructure and the strength–ductility response of such low-density steels; this condition is the low-TB (300 °C, just above Ms = 277 °C) counterpart of S1's 350 °C treatment.
unmapped: For the retained-austenite determination of S1 the paper uses equation (1), Vγ = (1 − Vc)(Iγ/Rγ)/[(Iα/Rα) + (Iγ/Rγ)], with the carbide fraction Vc taken from MatCalc equilibrium diagrams and (1 − Vc) = 0.78 marked for S1 in the TB = 300–350 °C band (Fig. 2).
S1's XRD pattern shows (111)γ, (110)α, (200)γ, (200)α, (220)γ, (211)α, (311)γ and (220)α reflections; the integrated (200)γ intensity Iγ illustrates the Vγ determination method.

The figure panels used to determine Bt are annotated with TB = 300 °C/Bt = 3600 s for S2 and the 1150 °C/300–350 °C TTP panel is described as S1 and approximately representative of S2; these contextual values belong to sibling samples (S2) rather than to S1 itself.
